title: Modern Web Development with JavaScript and TypeScript in WebStorm
subtitle: Build interactive web pages and a small Node.js back end with JavaScript and TypeScript, then test and debug them in WebStorm.
outcomes: Set up JavaScript and TypeScript projects with Node.js and npm in WebStorm, and run, test and debug them there
Write modern JavaScript with values, functions, arrays, objects and modules
Make web pages interactive with the DOM and events, and load data with fetch and async/await
Add types with TypeScript, from interfaces and union types to generics, checked as you type
Build a small JSON API with Node.js and Express, and test it with Vitest
prerequisites: None: this course starts from zero, though it helps to have seen a little HTML. You need a Windows, macOS or Linux computer with Node.js (the LTS version from nodejs.org), a modern browser such as Chrome, Edge or Firefox, and WebStorm, which is free for non-commercial use such as learning.
description: Learn to build for the web the way professional developers do: in WebStorm, an IDE that understands JavaScript and TypeScript. Each lesson teaches an idea and then shows it in WebStorm, step by step, with the keyboard shortcuts for macOS, Windows and Linux. You'll start with the core of JavaScript, run it with Node.js and organise it into modules. Then you'll make pages that respond to clicks and forms and load data with fetch, and add TypeScript so that mistakes show up as you type rather than when your users find them. Finally you'll build a small JSON API with Node.js and Express, test it with Vitest and debug it with breakpoints. Every module ends with a hands-on lab that you submit for your instructor's feedback, and the course ends with a small web app, front end and back end, that you build yourself.

modules.title: JavaScript fundamentals with Node.js
modules.summary: Set up WebStorm and Node.js, then learn the core of JavaScript, from values and functions to arrays, objects and modules, by writing and running small programs.

lessons.title: JavaScript, Node.js and your first project
objectives: Explain where JavaScript runs: in browsers and in Node.js
Create a WebStorm project with a package.json and run a script with Node.js
key_points: JavaScript is the programming language of the web: every browser runs it. Node.js runs JavaScript outside the browser, which is how it's used for servers, command-line tools and build tools.
npm, which comes with Node.js, installs packages from the npm registry; a project's package.json records its name, its scripts and the packages it depends on.
npm install puts packages in a node_modules folder and records their exact versions in package-lock.json, so everyone gets the same ones; node_modules isn't committed to version control.
"type": "module" in package.json makes Node.js treat .js files as ES modules, the modern standard that uses import and export.
WebStorm understands JavaScript and TypeScript without extra set-up: it completes code, points out mistakes as you type, and runs, tests and debugs your code.

walkthrough.title: Create a project and run a script

steps.do: Install Node.js, the LTS version from nodejs.org. Then, on WebStorm's Welcome screen, click New Project, choose Empty Project, name it js-basics and click Create.
Check that WebStorm found Node.js: open Settings and go to Languages & Frameworks | Node.js, where Node interpreter shows its version.
Open the Terminal and create a package.json file.

steps.do: Open package.json and make the project use ES modules: add "type": "module" as a top-level property, or change it to "module" if npm wrote "commonjs".
In the Project tool window, select the project folder and create a JavaScript file named hello.js.
Run it: right-click in the editor and choose Run 'hello.js', or use the shortcut.

lessons.title: Values, variables and functions
objectives: Declare variables with const and let, and use JavaScript's basic types
Write functions as declarations and as arrow functions
key_points: Declare variables with const when they won't be reassigned and with let when they will; the older var has confusing scoping rules and is best avoided.
JavaScript's primitive types are number, string, boolean, undefined, null, bigint and symbol. typeof tells you which a value is, although typeof null is "object", a long-standing quirk.
Compare with === and !==: == converts types first, so 0 == "" is true, while 0 === "" is false.
Template literals, written in backticks, put values into text: `Total: ${total.toFixed(2)}`.
Functions can be declared with function or written as arrow functions, as in const double = (n) => n * 2; parameters can have defaults, as in function greet(name = "world").

?? supplies a default only when a value is null or undefined, while || also replaces 0 and "". ?. (optional chaining) gives undefined instead of an error when something on the way is null or undefined.

Put the caret on toFixed and read its documentation, which WebStorm shows from MDN.
Put the caret on the string concatenation and open Show Context Actions: WebStorm offers to turn it into a template literal.

lessons.title: Arrays, objects and modules
objectives: Work with arrays and objects, including map, filter and reduce
Split code into ES modules with export and import
key_points: An array holds values in order: const scores = [88, 92, 79]; scores.length is 3, scores[0] is 88, and scores.push(100) adds a value to the end.
map, filter and reduce make new values from an array without a loop: scores.filter((s) => s > 80).map((s) => s * 2), and scores.reduce((sum, s) => sum + s, 0) adds them up.
An object groups named properties: const user = { name: "Ana", age: 31 }; user.name reads one, and destructuring, as in const { name } = user, unpacks it into a variable.
Spread syntax copies into a new array or object, as in [...scores, 70] or { ...user, age: 32 }; JSON.stringify and JSON.parse convert between values and JSON text.

A module exports what other files may use, as in export function total(items) { ... }, and other files import it: import { total } from "./cart.js". In Node.js, relative imports need the file extension.

steps.do: Create cart.js, which exports a function.
Create main.js. Type total and choose it from the completion list: WebStorm adds the import line for you.
Run main.js.

modules.title: The DOM, events and fetch
modules.summary: Make web pages interactive: find and change elements in the DOM, respond to clicks and forms, and load data with fetch and async/await without freezing the page.

lessons.title: HTML, the DOM and changing a page
objectives: Explain what the DOM is
Select, create and change elements with JavaScript
key_points: The browser turns an HTML page into the DOM (Document Object Model): a tree of objects, one for each element, that JavaScript can read and change.
document.querySelector("#tips") returns the first element that matches a CSS selector, or null if none does; querySelectorAll returns all the matches.
textContent sets an element's text safely. innerHTML parses its value as HTML, so never use it with text that came from a user or a server, which could inject scripts.
document.createElement("li") makes an element, append adds it to the page, and classList.add, remove and toggle change its CSS classes.
<script type="module" src="app.js"></script> loads a script as a module, which runs after the HTML has been parsed, so the elements it looks for already exist.

walkthrough.title: Build a page and open it from WebStorm

steps.do: Create index.html. Type ! and press Tab: the Emmet abbreviation expands into the skeleton of an HTML page.
Fill in the body.
Create app.js, which adds items to the list.

Open the page in a browser: hover over the top-right corner of the editor and click a browser's icon. WebStorm serves the page from its built-in web server, at an address that starts with http://localhost:63342/.

Open the browser's developer tools (F12 in Chrome, Edge and Firefox on Windows and Linux; Cmd+Option+I on macOS) and find the li elements your code created, in the Elements panel (Inspector in Firefox).
Back in WebStorm, put the caret on querySelector and read its documentation.

lessons.title: Events and forms
objectives: Respond to user actions with event listeners
Read and check form input without reloading the page
Debug browser code from WebStorm
key_points: element.addEventListener("click", handler) runs handler every time the event happens, passing it an event object that describes what happened.
A form's submit event fires when the user presses Enter or clicks its submit button; event.preventDefault() stops the browser from reloading the page, so your code can handle the form.
An input's value is always a string, even in a number input; convert it with Number(value) and check the result with Number.isNaN before using it.
Event delegation: one listener on a parent, such as a list, can handle clicks on all its children by looking at event.target, including children added later.
Common events are click, submit, input (the value changed), change, keydown and DOMContentLoaded (the HTML has been parsed).

steps.do: Add a form to index.html, above the list.
Handle the form's submit event in app.js.

Create a JavaScript Debug configuration: open Run | Edit Configurations, click +, choose JavaScript Debug, and paste the page's address from the browser into URL. WebStorm debugs in Chrome or another Chromium-based browser, such as Edge.
Click in the gutter beside event.preventDefault() to set a breakpoint, then debug the configuration.

Once the line that sets input has run, evaluate an expression in the paused page.

lessons.title: Asynchronous JavaScript and fetch
objectives: Explain the event loop, promises and async/await
Load JSON with fetch and handle errors properly
key_points: JavaScript runs your code on one thread. Slow work, such as timers and network requests, happens in the background, and its callback is queued to run once the current code has finished: this is the event loop.
A Promise stands for a result that isn't ready yet: it's pending, then either fulfilled with a value or rejected with an error, and then and catch register what to do in each case.
An async function always returns a promise. Inside it, await pauses that function, not the whole page, until a promise settles, and try/catch handles a rejection like any other error.
fetch(url) returns a promise of a Response: response.ok is true for status codes 200 to 299, and response.json() returns a promise of the parsed body.
fetch only rejects when the request can't be made at all, for example when the network is down. An HTTP error such as 404 still resolves, so check response.ok yourself.
Start independent requests together and wait for all of them with await Promise.all([a, b]), instead of awaiting each one in turn.

modules.title: TypeScript
modules.summary: Add types to JavaScript with TypeScript: set up the compiler, describe data with interfaces and union types, use generics, and let WebStorm catch mistakes before the code ever runs.

lessons.title: Why TypeScript, and setting it up
objectives: Explain what TypeScript adds to JavaScript
Set up a TypeScript project with tsconfig.json, and compile and run it
key_points: TypeScript is JavaScript with static types: you describe what values should look like, and the compiler, tsc, reports mistakes before the code runs, then outputs plain JavaScript.
Types are removed when the code is compiled, so they cost nothing at run time, but it also means they can't check data that arrives while the program runs, such as a JSON response.
tsconfig.json configures the compiler: which files to compile (rootDir and include), where the output goes (outDir), what kind of JavaScript to produce (target and module) and how strict to be.
"strict": true turns on the checks that matter most, including strictNullChecks, which makes null and undefined types of their own that code must handle.
Install TypeScript in each project as a development dependency, with npm install --save-dev typescript, and run it with npx tsc, so everyone on the project uses the same version.

steps.do: In a new project with a package.json that has "type": "module", open the Terminal and install TypeScript and the type definitions for Node.js.
Create tsconfig.json in the project's top-level folder.
Create src/hello.ts with a mistake in it.

steps.do: Open the Problems tool window to see the file's errors in a list.

lessons.title: Types, interfaces and unions
objectives: Annotate variables, parameters and return values
Describe objects with interfaces and choices with union types
Narrow a union safely before using it
key_points: Annotate with a colon, as in function total(prices: number[]): number. TypeScript infers most other types from values, so annotations matter most on parameters and return types.

An interface describes an object's shape: interface Track { title: string; seconds: number; artist?: string }, where ? marks an optional property. A type alias, such as type Seconds = number, names any type.
A union type allows one of several types, as in string | number, and a union of literal types lists the allowed values: type Topic = "naming" | "testing" | "git".
Narrowing: inside if (typeof value === "string"), TypeScript knows value is a string. Checking a shared property, such as kind, narrows a union of object types in the same way.
unknown is the safe type for values you haven't checked yet, such as parsed JSON: you must narrow it before using it. any switches type checking off, so avoid it.

steps.do: Write an interface and a function that uses it.
Create a Track that's missing properties. WebStorm underlines it, and Show Context Actions offers to add the missing properties.
Put the caret on a variable that has no annotation and read the type TypeScript inferred for it.
Write a function over a union of literal types, leaving one case out.
steps.see: An error: the function lacks an ending return statement, because the "git" case is missing.

steps.do: Add the missing case, then rename the title property in the interface: every use of it is updated.

lessons.title: Generics and typing real code
objectives: Write and use generic functions and types
Type asynchronous code, and data from outside the program
key_points: Generics let a function or type work with any type while remembering which one: function first<T>(items: T[]): T | undefined returns a string when it's given a string[].
Built-in generic types include Array<T>, usually written T[], Promise<T>, Map<K, V> and Record<K, V>, an object type whose keys are K and whose values are V.
Utility types make new types from existing ones: Partial<T> makes every property optional, Pick<T, K> keeps some properties and Omit<T, K> leaves some out.

An async function's return type is a promise, as in async function loadTips(): Promise<Tip[]>. TypeScript can't know the shape of a JSON response, so give it a type yourself, ideally after checking the data.
Type definitions for JavaScript libraries come with the library or from an @types package, such as @types/node for Node.js's own modules.

steps.do: Write a generic function and call it with two kinds of array. Put the caret on each result to see the type TypeScript worked out.
steps.see: word is string | undefined and n is number | undefined.

steps.do: Write a generic function that counts items into a Record.

modules.title: A Node.js back end, testing and debugging
modules.summary: Build a small JSON API with Node.js and Express in TypeScript, try it with WebStorm's HTTP Client, test its rules with Vitest and debug it with breakpoints.

lessons.title: A JSON API with Node.js and Express
objectives: Build an HTTP API with Express routes that receive and send JSON
Answer with the right status codes, and validate input
Try an API with WebStorm's HTTP Client
key_points: Express is a small web framework for Node.js: const app = express(); app.get("/api/tasks", (req, res) => { res.json(tasks); }); app.listen(3000); serves JSON at http://localhost:3000/api/tasks.
A route matches an HTTP method and a path. Path parameters, as in /api/tasks/:id, arrive in req.params as strings, and the query string in req.query.
app.use(express.json()) parses JSON request bodies into req.body, and app.use(express.static("public")) serves a front end's files from the same server.
Answer with the right status code: 200 OK, 201 Created for something new, 400 Bad Request for invalid input and 404 Not Found, as in res.status(404).json({ error: "Task not found" }).
Check every request body on the server, even if the page checks it too, because anyone can send any request to an API.
WebStorm's HTTP Client sends requests written in .http files, so you can try an API without leaving the IDE.

lessons.title: Testing with Vitest in WebStorm
objectives: Write unit tests with Vitest
Run tests and read their results in WebStorm
key_points: Vitest is a test runner for JavaScript and TypeScript: install it with npm install --save-dev vitest, put tests in files whose names end in .test.ts, and run them with npx vitest run.
A test file groups tests with describe and defines each with it (or test), using expect to state what must be true: expect(validateTitle(" a ")).toBe("a").
toBe compares with Object.is, which suits numbers and strings; toEqual compares the contents of objects and arrays; toThrow checks that a function throws.
Keep the rules in plain functions or classes, separate from Express's request handling, so they can be tested quickly without starting a server.
Vitest runs TypeScript test files directly, without a build step, and WebStorm shows a run icon beside each test and the difference between the expected and received values when one fails.

lessons.title: Debugging Node.js and TypeScript in WebStorm
objectives: Debug a Node.js server and its tests in WebStorm
Use source maps to debug TypeScript, and conditional breakpoints to stop at the right moment
key_points: WebStorm's debugger works with Node.js programs, npm scripts and tests: set breakpoints, start with Debug instead of Run, and the program pauses at them.
"sourceMap": true in tsconfig.json makes the compiler write .map files that link the JavaScript back to your TypeScript, so breakpoints and stepping work in the .ts files.
While the program is paused, the Variables pane shows the values in scope, Evaluate Expression runs any expression, and the Frames list shows how execution got there.
A conditional breakpoint stops only when its condition is true; a breakpoint with Suspend turned off and a message to log works like a console.log you never have to delete.
Debugging a single failing test from its run icon is often the quickest way to see why it fails.

steps.do: Run build, then click the arrow beside the start script in package.json and choose Debug.
steps.see: The server starts under the debugger.

steps.do: Put a breakpoint on the first line of the POST route's handler in server.ts.
Send the POST request from requests.http. WebStorm stops at the breakpoint in your TypeScript: look at req.body in the Variables pane.
Step over the handler's lines.
Evaluate an expression in the paused server.
Right-click the breakpoint and give it a condition, so it only stops for requests without a title.
Resume the program.
Debug a single test: click the icon beside a test in tasks.test.ts and choose Debug.

lab.title: Build, test and debug a tasks API
lab.goal: Build a small tasks API with Express and TypeScript, with its rules in a separate module tested with Vitest: list tasks, add a task, mark one done, and reject bad requests with the right status codes.
setup: The starter project: package.json, tsconfig.json, requests.http, and src/tasks.ts, src/tasks.test.ts and src/server.ts

steps.do: Open the starter project in WebStorm and install its packages in the Terminal.
Run the tests with the arrow beside the test script in package.json.
steps.see: One test passes and two fail, because add doesn't exist yet.

steps.do: Write add in tasks.ts, then rerun the tests.
steps.see: All three tests pass.

steps.do: Write the three tests listed in the TODO in tasks.test.ts, then write complete to make them pass.
Write the two POST routes in server.ts, using the TaskList and catching ValidationError.
Run build, then start, with the arrows beside them in package.json.
steps.see: Listening on http://localhost:3000

steps.do: Open requests.http and send each request in turn with the arrow beside it.
steps.see: 200 OK, then 201 Created, 400 Bad Request, 200 OK with done: true, and 404 Not Found.

steps.do: Stop the server, then debug the start script (the last configuration you ran). Put a breakpoint in the POST /api/tasks route, send the request without a title, and step through to the 400 response.
Run the tests once more in the Terminal.
steps.see: 6 passed

checks.text: Adding a task answers 201 Created with the new task.
A blank title is rejected with 400 Bad Request and a clear message.
Marking a task done works, and an unknown id gives 404 Not Found.
The rules live in tasks.ts, tested without starting the server, and the routes use them.

lab.submit: Paste tasks.ts, tasks.test.ts and server.ts, the summary from npm test, and the status line of each response from requests.http.

files.content:
### List the tasks
GET http://localhost:3000/api/tasks

### Add a task
POST http://localhost:3000/api/tasks
Content-Type: application/json

{"title": "Write the API"}

### Add a task without a title
POST http://localhost:3000/api/tasks
Content-Type: application/json

{"title": "   "}

### Mark task 1 done
POST http://localhost:3000/api/tasks/1/done

### Mark a task that doesn't exist
POST http://localhost:3000/api/tasks/99/done

hints: Express gives path parameters as strings: Number(req.params.id) turns "1" into 1.
In a catch block, error is unknown until you narrow it: if (error instanceof ValidationError) { ... }.
If start runs old code, run build first: start runs the compiled JavaScript in dist.

project.title: Build a small web app: an event sign-up board
project.brief: Build a small web app for a community group's events, with a TypeScript back end and a page that uses it. The server, built with Node.js and Express, keeps a list of events (a title, a date and a number of places) and answers JSON: it lists the events, shows one, and signs someone up with a name and an email address. It rejects bad input, a full event and an email that has already signed up, with the right status codes and clear messages, and keeps its data in a JSON file so it survives a restart. The page, served by the same server, lists the events with the places left, lets visitors sign up with a form, and shows success and error messages without reloading, using fetch and async/await. Keep the rules in plain TypeScript functions or classes tested with Vitest, try the API with WebStorm's HTTP Client, and use the debugger to fix whatever doesn't work.
deliverables: The project: package.json, tsconfig.json and the TypeScript source of the server, with the rules in a module of their own
The front end (HTML, CSS and JavaScript or TypeScript), served by the same server and using fetch, events and the DOM
At least eight Vitest tests of the rules, including a full event and a repeated email address
A requests.http file that tries every endpoint, including the error cases
A README.md that explains how to install, build, run and test the app
Screenshots or a description of the page in use, and the npm test summary

rubric.name: It works
rubric.description: Events are listed with the places left, sign-ups are saved and survive a restart, and the page and the API agree.

rubric.name: API design
rubric.description: Clear routes, JSON in and out, and the right status codes (200, 201, 400, 404, and 409 Conflict for a full event or a repeated email) with helpful messages.

rubric.name: Front end
rubric.description: The page uses fetch with async/await, shows errors visibly, updates without reloading, and uses textContent rather than innerHTML for data.

rubric.name: TypeScript
rubric.description: Strict mode with no errors, interfaces for the data, and no any where a real type would do.

rubric.name: Tests
rubric.description: At least eight meaningful Vitest tests of the rules, covering normal cases, edge cases and errors, all passing.

rubric.name: Readability and README
rubric.description: Consistent formatting, clear names, and a README that explains how to install, build, run and test the app.

project.submit: Paste your source files (each with its path), requests.http, your README, the npm test summary, and a description or screenshots of the page in use. A link to a public repository is welcome too.
